case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title I of the Americans with Disabilities Act allows a former employee (no longer able to perform the job) to sue an ex-employer for disability discrimination in a post-employment benefits policy.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title I of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (42 U.S.C. § 12101 et seq.), particularly the provisions governing who may sue (the 'qualified individual' concept) and enforcement via the Title VII remedial framework incorporated through 42 U.S.C. § 12117(a) (incorporating 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Stanley argues that Title I’s anti-discrimination protections and remedies extend to discrimination affecting former employees in post-employment benefits (such as disability-retirement or similar fringe benefits), and that requiring a plaintiff to be a currently 'qualified individual' at the time of the challenged post-employment benefit denial would improperly create a loophole allowing employers to discriminate in benefits precisely when disability makes continued employment impossible.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The City of Sanford argues (consistent with Eleventh Circuit precedent referenced in the record) that Title I’s protection is limited to a 'qualified individual'—i.e., someone who can perform the essential functions of the job with or without reasonable accommodation—and that a former employee who is no longer working (and not seeking to work) cannot satisfy that requirement and therefore cannot bring an ADA Title I claim challenging post-employment benefits decisions.
key_precedents: Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997)
Gonzales v. Garner Food Services, Inc. (11th Cir. precedent referenced as controlling in the Eleventh Circuit materials)
Johnson v. K Mart Corp., 273 F.3d 1035 (11th Cir. 2001) (vacated)
Johnson v. K Mart Corp., 281 F.3d 1368 (11th Cir. 2002) (en banc) (appeal dismissed after vacatur/settlement)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the best point: § 12111(8)’s present-tense, job-performance definition of “qualified individual” makes a categorical post-separation suit look textually difficult, and Robinson involved an undefined term in Title VII. But even accepting that structural ordering matters, Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan are right that reading “qualified” as a time-of-suit gate effectively drains § 12112(a)’s express coverage of discrimination in “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment” for deferred benefits—an evasion opportunity Congress did not clearly create. The narrower reconciliation, consistent with my institutional and minimalist approach, is to tether Title I to the employment relationship: former employees may sue only over denial of benefits earned as part of compensation during the period they were qualified, without converting Title I into a general post-employment code. Justice Alito is correct that § 12117(a) does not expand substantive coverage, but it reinforces that Congress expected the Title I scheme to operate coherently for employment benefits that predictably mature after separation.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest opposing argument is Chief Justice Roberts’s “remedial gap/evasion” concern, echoed by Justices Kagan, Barrett, and Kavanaugh, that a present-tense reading of “qualified individual” would hollow out “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment” for deferred benefits. But under the statute’s text and structure, § 12112(a) first limits the protected class to discrimination “against a qualified individual,” and § 12111(8) then defines that class in present-tense, job-performance terms; Roberts’s proposed “qualified when benefits were earned” rule replaces Congress’s definition with a judicially crafted temporal proxy. Robinson v. Shell Oil does not undermine this conclusion because it addressed ambiguity in Title VII’s undefined “employees,” whereas here Congress spoke directly by supplying a narrowing definition that forecloses treating former employees as “qualified individuals” based on past capacity. Any resulting policy gap for post-employment benefit administration cannot justify detaching Title I’s substantive prohibition from its express predicate; that is a choice for Congress, not this Court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed “benefits earned while qualified” rule is the most thoughtful attempt to avoid what Justice Kagan calls a remedial gap, but it still asks us to treat § 12111(8)’s present-tense, job-performance definition as a past-tense status test keyed to some earlier period—an atextual carveout that Congress did not write. The “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment” language in § 12112(a) does real work, but it cannot override the statute’s threshold limitation that the challenged discrimination must be “against a qualified individual”; accepting Roberts’s harmonization inverts that structure by using a downstream phrase to expand an upstream limitation. Robinson v. Shell Oil does not undermine this conclusion because, as Justice Thomas notes, Robinson resolved ambiguity in Title VII’s undefined “employees,” whereas here Congress supplied an explicit, narrowing definition that courts are not free to relax to prevent evasion. If that leaves some post-employment benefits disputes outside Title I, that is a consequence of the text as enacted, not a license for judicial revision.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the strongest point: § 12111(8)’s present-tense, job-performance definition of “qualified individual” and the rule that § 12117(a) cannot expand substantive coverage. But that textual premise does not resolve the distinct question raised by § 12112(a)’s express regulation of discrimination in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” which includes deferred benefits whose administration predictably occurs after separation; treating “qualified” as a time-of-suit gate would, as Chief Justice Roberts notes, invite easy timing-based evasion that makes the statute self-defeating in a core compensation context. Robinson v. Shell Oil is not being used to override clear text (as Justice Alito fears), but to reinforce a harmonizing canon: we should avoid a reading that drains “privileges of employment” of practical effect for earned benefits disputes tethered to the employment relationship. Roberts’s narrow approach—assessing “qualified” during the benefit-earning employment period and limiting coverage to employment-rooted benefits—best reconciles the provisions while preserving the statute’s real-world protection for disabled workers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right that § 12111(8)’s present-tense, job-performance definition is a serious textual constraint, and Robinson can’t be used to override clear limiting language. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, reading “qualified” as an absolute time-of-suit gate makes § 12112(a)’s coverage of “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment” strangely ineffectual for deferred or administered-after-separation benefits—an ordinary slice of compensation—and invites the timing-based evasion Roberts identifies. Under my pragmatic textualism, the better reconciliation is Roberts’s narrow, employment-tethered rule: the challenged act must concern benefits earned as part of employment compensation, and “qualified” is assessed at the relevant employment period when that term/benefit attached, not as a free-floating post-employment status test. Justice Alito is correct that § 12117(a) can’t expand substantive coverage, but its incorporation of Title VII’s scheme supports reading Title I coherently to reach post-separation administration of earned employment benefits rather than creating a remedial dead zone.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s proposed “benefits earned while qualified” limitation is the most serious attempt at harmonization, but it still rewrites § 12111(8)’s definition from a present-tense capacity-to-perform requirement into a backward-looking status inquiry whenever benefits are at issue. As Justice Thomas explains, Robinson v. Shell Oil turned on ambiguity in Title VII’s undefined “employees”; here Congress supplied an express narrowing definition, and § 12117(a)’s remedial cross-reference cannot enlarge the substantive class protected by § 12112(a). Justice Kagan’s remedial-gap/evasion concern is intuitive, yet under a textualist separation-of-powers approach it cannot justify creating a judicial carveout that detaches Title I from its job-performance predicate. If deferred-benefits administration truly falls through the cracks, that policy choice is for Congress to correct, not for us to cure by adopting a time-of-earning gloss absent from the enacted text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the best point for respondent: § 12111(8)’s present-tense definition of “qualified individual” cannot simply be rewritten into a past-tense status test, and Robinson involved an undefined term. But Chief Justice Roberts’s approach does not discard the job-performance predicate; it reads “qualified” to apply at the relevant employment/benefit-earning period for disputes over “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” avoiding an interpretation that effectively lets an employer evade Title I by postponing a discriminatory benefits decision until after separation. Justice Alito is right that § 12117(a) does not expand substantive coverage, yet the cross-reference reinforces that Congress expected the enforcement scheme to operate in the common setting of post-separation administration of earned benefits, which makes a rigid time-of-suit bar an awkward fit with § 12112(a)’s text. Under an institutionalist, text-and-structure method, the narrow, employment-tethered construction best harmonizes these provisions without turning Title I into a free-floating post-employment code.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch forcefully argue that § 12112(a)’s prohibition is limited to discrimination “against a qualified individual,” and that § 12111(8)’s present-tense, job-performance definition forecloses a former-employee claim; that is the hardest textual point. But I do not read § 12111(8) to answer, by itself, the distinct question whether discrimination in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment” includes the post-separation administration of benefits that were part of the compensation package when the plaintiff was employed and qualified—Chief Justice Roberts’s employment-tethered rule best harmonizes those phrases without converting Title I into a free-floating post-employment code. Justice Alito is right that § 12117(a) cannot expand substantive coverage, yet it still supports reading Title I to function coherently for a predictable class of employment benefits disputes rather than creating an evasion-by-timing loophole that drains “privileges of employment” of ordinary meaning for deferred benefits. Robinson is not controlling (as Thomas notes), but its scheme-based caution against self-defeating constructions reinforces that the more faithful reconciliation is to assess “qualified” with reference to the relevant employment period for earned benefits rather than as an absolute time-of-suit gate.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that § 12111(8)’s present-tense, job-performance definition of “qualified individual” forecloses any post-separation claim—has real force, but it assumes the temporal question is answered by grammar alone and disregards how § 12112(a) expressly reaches “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” including deferred benefits whose administration predictably occurs after employment ends. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, a categorical time-of-suit bar would invite straightforward evasion by timing disability-based benefit denials to separation, effectively hollowing out Congress’s inclusion of employment benefits in the operative prohibition. Robinson v. Shell Oil is relevant not to expand substance via procedure (contra Justice Alito), but as a contextual interpretive reminder that employment statutes should not be read to make their remedial scheme self-defeating when the regulated employment practice necessarily manifests post-employment. The narrow, employment-tethered approach—assessing “qualified” at the time the benefit attached to the job—best harmonizes the provisions while preserving § 12111(8)’s job-performance anchor and limiting Title I to disputes rooted in the prior employment relationship.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title I’s enforcement provision, 42 U.S.C. § 12117(a), incorporates Title VII’s remedial framework, which this Court has read to “necessarily refer[] to former employees” who must be able to invoke those remedies. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), held that statutory terms like “employees” can include former employees where excluding them would create a remedial gap inconsistent with the overall scheme; the same structural logic applies here to post-employment benefits decisions that arise only after separation. Reading “qualified individual” to categorically bar any former employee from challenging discriminatory benefit policies would create a loophole—precisely when disability ends employment—without clear textual command in § 12112(a) or § 12111(8). A narrow holding can recognize standing for former employees to challenge discrimination in benefits earned through employment, without converting Title I into a general post-employment code untethered to the employment relationship.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Title I’s operative prohibition applies only to discrimination “against a qualified individual on the basis of disability,” 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), and the statute defines “qualified individual” in present-tense functional terms as someone who “can perform the essential functions” of the job, § 12111(8). A former employee who is no longer able to perform (and is not seeking to perform) the job cannot satisfy that textual prerequisite, so Title I does not authorize suit over a post-employment benefits policy in these circumstances. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), construed the ambiguous term “employees” in Title VII’s anti-retaliation provision to include former employees, but it did not confront (and cannot override) the ADA’s explicit “qualified individual” limitation. Although § 12117(a) incorporates Title VII’s enforcement mechanism, it does not expand the class of plaintiffs beyond those covered by Title I’s substantive text.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title I’s operative prohibition is limited to discrimination “against a qualified individual on the basis of disability,” and a “qualified individual” is one who “can perform the essential functions” of the job with or without reasonable accommodation. 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a); § 12111(8). A former employee who concedes he can no longer perform the job is outside that defined class, and the incorporation of Title VII’s remedial framework via § 12117(a) cannot expand the ADA’s substantive coverage beyond Congress’s express “qualified individual” limitation. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), turned on ambiguity in Title VII’s use of “employees” in an anti-retaliation provision; here, Congress supplied an unambiguous temporal and functional qualifier—“qualified”—that forecloses extending Title I to non-qualified ex-employees for post-employment benefits disputes.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title I’s substantive ban on discrimination in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” including fringe benefits, 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), would be undermined if an employer could evade liability simply because disability later renders the worker unable to perform the job at the moment benefits are denied. Through § 12117(a), Congress incorporated Title VII’s enforcement scheme (42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5), which this Court in Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), read to contemplate suits by former employees—otherwise the remedial framework would contain a glaring loophole for post-employment retaliation or discrimination. Reading “qualified individual” to bar all former-employee benefits claims would strip protection from a particularly vulnerable group (those whose disabilities ended their employment) and would invite discriminatory structuring of deferred compensation. The better construction is that “qualified individual” is satisfied when the discrimination relates to compensation earned through employment and the plaintiff was qualified during the relevant employment relationship, even if no longer able to work when the benefit is withheld.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title I’s substantive prohibition covers discrimination by a covered “employer” in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” which naturally includes fringe benefits that were earned through the employment relationship even if administered post-employment. Reading the “qualified individual” definition to bar any suit the moment a disability ends active service would create a significant loophole inconsistent with the statute’s coherent operation and its integration of Title VII’s enforcement scheme through 42 U.S.C. § 12117(a) (incorporating 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5). Robinson v. Shell Oil teaches that, where the remedial framework plainly contemplates post-employment disputes, the covered class is best read to include former employees absent clear temporal limitation; nothing in Title I’s enforcement provisions indicates Congress meant to foreclose claims about discriminatory benefit policies that flow from prior employment. This construction is also more workable administratively, allowing courts and agencies to police discrimination in benefits without forcing artificial “current qualification” inquiries disconnected from the benefit decision.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Title I’s operative prohibition applies to discrimination against a “qualified individual,” defined as a person who “can perform the essential functions” of the job with or without accommodation, 42 U.S.C. §§ 12112(a), 12111(8). A former employee who concedes he cannot perform the job is outside that unambiguous limitation, and courts may not rewrite the statute to reach sympathetic cases, especially where doing so would expand liability beyond the line Congress drew. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), construed Title VII’s term “employees” in an anti-retaliation provision that lacked a temporal qualifier and was therefore ambiguous; here, the “qualified individual” requirement supplies the relevant temporal/functional limitation and forecloses Robinson’s path. Although § 12117(a) incorporates Title VII’s remedial framework, it does not enlarge the class protected beyond those Title I expressly covers, and separation-of-powers principles counsel against using remedial cross-references to override clear substantive limits.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title I’s enforcement provision, 42 U.S.C. § 12117(a), incorporates Title VII’s remedial framework, and Robinson v. Shell Oil Co. teaches that employment-discrimination statutes are ordinarily read to permit former employees to invoke those remedies for post-employment discrimination when the statutory scheme otherwise contemplates such suits. Reading the ADA to categorically bar former employees from challenging discriminatory post-employment benefits would create a practical and administrable loophole: employers could lawfully discriminate in fringe benefits precisely when a worker becomes disabled and exits employment, undermining Title I’s prohibition on discrimination in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment.” While § 12111(8)’s “qualified individual” language limits who can demand accommodation for performing a job, it need not be read to strip standing to challenge discrimination in benefits earned as part of employment, especially where the discriminatory policy operates after separation. This construction best harmonizes text, precedent, and workability while avoiding a destabilizing narrowing of settled anti-discrimination remedies.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title I’s substantive prohibition reaches discrimination in “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), and fringe or retirement benefits are a paradigmatic “privilege” that often vests or is administered only after employment ends. The enforcement provision, § 12117(a), incorporates Title VII’s remedial scheme in 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5, which—like the provisions at issue in Robinson—contemplates suits by former employees (e.g., reinstatement and other relief necessarily pursued post-separation), making it textually coherent to allow former employees to invoke the remedial mechanisms for post-employment discrimination. Although the ADA defines a “qualified individual” as one who can perform the job’s essential functions, § 12111(8), that definition is best read to limit who may claim discrimination “in regard to … discharge” or other job-performance-linked decisions, not to create a loophole immunizing discriminatory administration of earned post-employment benefits. Reading “qualified individual” to categorically bar such suits would be methodologically inconsistent with Robinson’s insistence that statutory terms be construed in light of the whole remedial structure and the practical operation of employment statutes.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title I’s enforcement provision, 42 U.S.C. § 12117(a), incorporates Title VII’s remedial framework, and Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), instructs that statutory references to “employees” can encompass former employees where needed to avoid undermining the statute’s anti-discrimination purpose. Reading the ADA’s “qualified individual” definition (42 U.S.C. § 12111(8)) to categorically bar suits by former employees challenging discriminatory post-employment benefits would create a practical loophole: employers could deny disability-linked benefits precisely when a worker becomes unable to perform the job, insulating discrimination in compensation and “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment.” Procedural fairness and statutory function favor allowing claims tied to benefits earned as part of the employment relationship even if paid or administered post-employment. This interpretation aligns with the ADA’s broad mandate to eliminate disability discrimination, 42 U.S.C. § 12101(b)(1), while leaving merits defenses (e.g., whether the benefit policy is discriminatory) to be litigated under the incorporated Title VII procedures.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title I of the Americans with Disabilities Act allows a former employee to sue a former employer for disability discrimination in post-employment benefits (e.g., retirement or pension-related benefits), or whether the plaintiff must be a current “qualified individual” at the time of the challenged benefits decision.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title I of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a) (prohibiting discrimination against a “qualified individual on the basis of disability” in employment terms/conditions/privileges, including benefits), and the ADA enforcement provision, 42 U.S.C. § 12117(a) (incorporating Title VII enforcement procedures in 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-5).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Stanley argues that Title I’s ban on discrimination in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment” necessarily reaches employer-controlled benefits decisions that occur after employment ends (such as pension/retirement benefits), because those benefits are earned through employment and are part of the employment relationship. She contends the Eleventh Circuit’s rule—requiring a plaintiff to be currently able to perform the job’s essential functions—creates a loophole that lets employers discriminate precisely when disability often arises (e.g., at or after retirement), conflicts with the ADA’s broad remedial purpose, and is inconsistent with Supreme Court guidance interpreting similar language in Title VII to cover former employees’ post-employment claims.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The City of Sanford argues that Title I’s text limits actionable discrimination to discrimination against a “qualified individual,” which it reads as requiring the person to be able to perform the essential functions of the job at the time of the challenged act. Because a retiree or former employee is not performing (and may not be able to perform) the job, the City contends they fall outside Title I’s protected class for purposes of challenging post-employment benefits decisions. The City relies on Eleventh Circuit precedent treating this “qualified individual” requirement as a jurisdictional/threshold limitation that bars suits over post-employment fringe benefits by former employees who are no longer qualified for (or seeking) the job.
key_precedents: Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997)

Gonzales v. Garner Food Services, Inc. (11th Cir. precedent referenced as establishing that a former employee cannot sue over post-employment benefits under Title I unless qualified/working/seeking work)
Johnson v. K Mart Corp., 273 F.3d 1035 (11th Cir. 2001) (panel decision reading Robinson to overrule Gonzales, later vacated)
Johnson v. K Mart Corp., 281 F.3d 1368 (11th Cir. 2002) (en banc) (vacatur/dismissal after settlement/bankruptcy; no en banc merits opinion)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s textual point remains the hardest: § 12112(a) reaches only discrimination “against a qualified individual,” and § 12111(8) defines that status by ability to perform essential functions. But that definition supplies a gatekeeping concept for employment-derived rights; it does not clearly impose a timing rule that extinguishes protection for “compensation” and “privileges of employment” the moment payment is administered post-separation, especially for deferred benefits earned through past qualified service. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Robinson v. Shell Oil is persuasive in method even if not controlling on identical text: we should avoid a reading that makes a core statutory phrase—benefits as “privileges of employment”—functionally inoperative and invites evasion. A narrow holding limited to employer-controlled administration of accrued, employment-earned benefits (not all post-employment disputes) both respects the “qualified” limitation and avoids the loophole Justice Sotomayor identifies, preserving institutional legitimacy through minimalism.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: I have considered Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s argument that reading “qualified individual” as a temporal bar would hollow out § 12112(a)’s reference to “compensation” and “privileges of employment,” especially for deferred retirement benefits. But the enacted text makes “qualified individual” a threshold condition for liability, and § 12111(8) defines that status by the ability to perform the job’s essential functions—language that, as written, does not naturally describe a retiree at the time of the challenged benefits decision. Robinson v. Shell Oil, invoked by Justice Kagan, is methodologically distinguishable because it resolved ambiguity in “employees” without a narrowing functional definition; here Congress supplied an explicit limiting definition, and we are not at liberty to relocate the “qualification” inquiry to some earlier moment simply to avoid a perceived loophole. However sensible the policy concerns, any extension to post-employment benefits administration untethered to present qualification must come from Congress, not judicial revision of statutory predicates.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s “privileges of employment/deferred compensation” argument is the strongest policy-and-structure case for Petitioners, but it still does not answer the statute’s threshold limitation: § 12112(a) prohibits discrimination only “against a qualified individual,” and § 12111(8) defines that term in present-tense, essential-functions language that cannot be treated as optional whenever a benefit is paid later. Robinson v. Shell Oil, as Justice Kagan stresses, is methodologically relevant, but it addressed an ambiguous term (“employees”) without an explicit functional definition; here Congress supplied that narrowing definition, and we should not use Robinson’s anti-evasion impulse to effectively rewrite who counts as protected under Title I. Petitioners’ proposed “earned-while-qualified” gloss (advanced by Roberts, Barrett, and Gorsuch) may be administrable, but it is not grounded in the enacted text, and it would expand Title I’s coverage to post-employment benefit disputes in a way Congress did not clearly authorize. If there is a loophole, it is for Congress to close, not for us to close by diluting the “qualified individual” requirement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s textual point about “qualified individual” (§§ 12112(a), 12111(8)) is the hardest, but it assumes the qualification inquiry must be pegged to the moment of the benefits decision rather than to the employment relationship that earned the deferred compensation; that timing rule is not in the text and would effectively erase “compensation” and “privileges of employment” for the many benefits that vest or pay out post-separation. As the Chief and Justice Kagan emphasize, Robinson’s contextual method matters here: we read employment-discrimination provisions to avoid making core protections practically self-defeating through formalistic timing, even if the definitional term differs. Justice Alito’s concern about rewriting the statute is answered by a narrow, administrable limit—coverage for employer-controlled administration of benefits accrued through past covered employment—so we respect “qualified” without creating a loophole that predictably harms disabled workers when they are most vulnerable. Under my pragmatic approach attentive to real-world effects and access to justice, the respondent’s reading invites evasion and undermines the statute’s remedial design without clear congressional command.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point remains that § 12112(a) is framed as discrimination “against a qualified individual,” with § 12111(8) defining “qualified” in essential-functions terms that sound present-tense and job-focused. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, treating that definition as a categorical temporal bar would make the same sentence’s protection for “compensation” and “privileges of employment” incoherent as to deferred benefits—classic employment privileges that, by design, are often administered post-separation. Justice Alito’s Robinson distinction has some force (the ADA has an added definition), but Robinson’s core contextual move still matters here: where the challenged act is tethered to the employment relationship, a rigid timing rule invites evasion and hollows out the statute’s benefits language without any clear textual command. A narrow, text-anchored rule—coverage for discriminatory administration of employer-controlled benefits accrued through covered, qualified employment—respects “qualified” as a screen while preserving statutory coherence.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas offers the sharpest textual objection: § 12112(a) reaches only a “qualified individual,” and § 12111(8) defines that term in present-tense, essential-functions language. But that definition answers who may complain about discrimination in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” and it does not itself supply an atextual timing rule that strips protection once compensation earned through qualified service is later administered post-separation. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, reading “qualified” to categorically exclude retirees would effectively nullify Congress’s express inclusion of “compensation” and “privileges of employment” for the very category of deferred benefits that vest or are paid after employment ends, without any clear statutory instruction to do so. Robinson is not on all fours, but Justice Kagan is right that its contextual method supports construing employment-discrimination provisions to reach post-employment acts tethered to the prior employment relationship when a contrary reading makes the operative protections self-defeating.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point remains that “qualified individual” in § 12111(8) is a real limiting definition tied to essential job functions, and we cannot treat it as surplusage. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett explain, using that definition as a categorical temporal bar for any post-employment benefits dispute would effectively nullify § 12112(a)’s express coverage of “compensation” and “privileges of employment” for deferred benefits—an implausible reading absent a clear timing cutoff in the text. Robinson v. Shell Oil is not controlling because the definitional scheme differs, yet its contextual method supports reading Title I to reach post-separation actions tethered to the employment relationship when otherwise the statute invites evasion. The administrable, text-anchored path is a narrow rule: the plaintiff must have been a “qualified individual” during the employment period when the benefit was earned, and the challenged discrimination must concern employer-controlled administration of that accrued privilege.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the best textual point: § 12112(a) reaches only discrimination “against a qualified individual,” and § 12111(8) defines “qualified” in essential-functions terms that, read literally at the moment of a post-employment benefits decision, would exclude retirees. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, that reading would effectively erase Congress’s inclusion of “compensation” and “privileges of employment” for a class of benefits—pensions and other deferred compensation—that are characteristically administered after separation, without any explicit temporal cutoff in the enacted text. The more faithful textual harmonization is to treat “qualified” as a threshold tied to the employment relationship that generated the benefit (i.e., the individual was qualified when earning/accruing it), and to limit liability to employer-controlled administration of employment-derived benefits, rather than importing a present-ability requirement that makes the “privileges” clause largely inoperative. Robinson is not dispositive on identical language, but its contextual method remains persuasive here because it confirms we should not infer a silent timing carveout that invites evasion when the statute’s own words (“privileges of employment”) point the other way.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s textual argument—that § 12112(a) reaches only a “qualified individual” as defined by current ability to perform essential job functions—has real force, but it assumes a timing rule the statute does not state and that sits uneasily with Congress’s express coverage of “compensation” and “privileges of employment,” which naturally includes deferred retirement benefits. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively show that importing a rigid present-ability screen into post-separation benefit administration would effectively nullify that clause and invite an administrable loophole: discriminate at the payout stage once the worker is off payroll. Robinson v. Shell Oil is not identical, as Justice Alito notes, but its contextual method still matters here: where a narrow reading would make the remedial scheme practically self-defeating, we should read coverage to include post-employment acts tethered to the employment relationship. Under my procedural-fairness and consequences-aware approach, the better harmonizing construction is that “qualified” is satisfied when the benefit was earned through covered employment and the challenged discrimination concerns employer-controlled administration of that earned privilege, not present capacity to perform a job the person no longer holds.

John Roberts.reasoning: Title I makes it unlawful to discriminate against a “qualified individual” in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), and employer-provided retirement and pension benefits are paradigmatic “privileges of employment” earned through the employment relationship even if administered after separation. Reading “qualified individual” to require present ability to perform the job at the time of a post-employment benefits decision would create a substantial loophole, allowing discrimination precisely in deferred compensation that was part of the bargain for past service, without clear textual command. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), supports the narrower, administrable rule that antidiscrimination provisions covering employment-related consequences can extend to former employees when the challenged conduct is tethered to the prior employment relationship; nothing in § 12112(a) expressly limits “privileges of employment” to the period of active employment. To preserve uniformity and institutional legitimacy, I would follow Robinson’s functional approach and allow suits at least where the benefit was earned during employment and the claim challenges discrimination in the employer’s administration of that accrued benefit.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Title I makes it unlawful to discriminate against “a qualified individual on the basis of disability,” 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), and it defines “qualified individual” as one who “can perform the essential functions” of the job with or without accommodation, 42 U.S.C. § 12111(8); that textual limitation naturally operates at the time of the challenged employment action and excludes a retiree no longer able (or seeking) to perform the job. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), construed the term “employee” in Title VII’s retaliation provision, but it did so because that term lacked a temporal qualifier and was ambiguous in context—whereas the ADA’s operative prohibition expressly narrows the protected class to “qualified” individuals, making Robinson’s reasoning inapposite. Although § 12112(a) mentions “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” including benefits, that general phrase cannot override the statute’s threshold restriction to “qualified” individuals, and any broader coverage for former employees must come from Congress, not judicial revision. The enforcement cross-reference in § 12117(a) (incorporating Title VII procedures) supplies remedies and process, not an expansion of the ADA’s substantive coverage beyond what § 12112(a) and § 12111(8) textually provide.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Title I’s operative prohibition reaches only discrimination against a “qualified individual,” 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), and that term is defined to require the ability to perform the job’s essential functions, § 12111(8)—a present-tense limitation that does not naturally fit a retiree challenging a post-employment benefits decision. Robinson v. Shell Oil construed Title VII’s term “employees” to include former employees only because the term lacked temporal cues and because Title VII’s remedial provisions necessarily contemplated former-employee suits; Title I’s added and explicit “qualified individual” requirement supplies the temporal and functional limitation missing in Robinson. Extending Title I to former employees for post-employment benefits would effectively sever the “qualified” limitation from the cause of action and expand liability beyond what the enacted text fairly bears, with significant practical consequences for employer-administered benefit plans. The proper avenue for such an expansion is Congress, not this Court.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Title I bars discrimination against a “qualified individual on the basis of disability” in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” which naturally includes employer-controlled retirement and pension benefits earned through employment. Reading the “qualified individual” definition, 42 U.S.C. § 12111(8), to require current ability to perform job functions at the time of a post-employment benefits decision would create a perverse loophole—allowing discrimination precisely when disability often manifests and when workers are most vulnerable—contrary to the ADA’s remedial purpose and its incorporation of Title VII enforcement, 42 U.S.C. § 12117(a). Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), instructs that anti-discrimination protections using employment-status terms should be construed to reach former employees where necessary to prevent evasion and to make the statute work in real-world settings. Because post-employment benefits are “privileges of employment” under § 12112(a), a former employee may sue for discriminatory administration of those benefits even after separation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Title I prohibits discrimination “in regard to … compensation … and other terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), language that naturally encompasses employer-controlled retirement and pension benefits that are earned through employment even if administered after separation. Reading “qualified individual” (defined in § 12111(8)) to bar all post-employment benefits claims would create a substantial textual and practical mismatch—turning an ability-to-perform screen aimed at current job performance into a loophole for discriminatory denial of accrued benefits—while undercutting statutory coherence between the benefits clause and the nondiscrimination mandate. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), supports interpreting employment-discrimination terms in context to include former employees where the challenged act is rooted in the employment relationship, and nothing in § 12112(a) supplies an unambiguous temporal limitation that would exclude former employees from protection as to employment-derived benefits. Because this is a straightforward application of the statute’s coverage to employment “privileges,” it does not depend on administrative deference under § 12117(a)’s enforcement incorporation.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 12112(a) prohibits discrimination against a “qualified individual” in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” language that naturally encompasses employer-controlled fringe benefits earned through the employment relationship even if administered after separation. Reading “qualified individual” to require present ability to perform job functions at the time of a post-employment benefits decision would make the statute self-defeating for retirement and pension benefits—benefits that, by their nature, are often enjoyed only after one no longer “holds” the job—without any clear temporal limitation in § 12112(a). As in Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), where the Court construed “employees” in Title VII to include former employees in part because the remedial scheme necessarily contemplates post-termination claims, the ADA’s incorporated enforcement provision, § 12117(a) (importing § 2000e-5 remedies), likewise presupposes claims that can be brought only by former employees. The Eleventh Circuit’s contrary rule elevates an atextual timing requirement over the statute’s ordinary meaning and structure, and should be rejected on separation-of-powers grounds.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Title I prohibits discrimination against a “qualified individual” in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), and employer-controlled retirement or pension benefits are a core “privilege of employment” earned through the employment relationship even if administered after separation. Interpreting the statute to categorically bar former employees from challenging discriminatory post-employment benefits decisions would create an atextual loophole and undermine workability by allowing discrimination precisely at the point benefits vest or are paid. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), though a Title VII case, supplies strong guidance: where the statute’s remedial scheme and workplace realities necessarily contemplate suits by former employees, the protected class language is best read to include them, and Title I’s incorporation of Title VII enforcement procedures, 42 U.S.C. § 12117(a), likewise presupposes former-employee enforcement. The better reading—consistent with history, tradition in employment-discrimination law, and judicial restraint—is that the “qualified individual” requirement addresses job-related discrimination during employment, not an absolute temporal bar to suits over post-employment benefits earned while working.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Title I prohibits discrimination “against a qualified individual” in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), and employer-provided retirement or pension benefits are most naturally read as “privileges of employment” even if the discriminatory administration occurs post-employment. Reading “qualified individual” to require current ability to perform essential job functions at the time of a benefits decision would sever the statute’s protection from benefits earned through past employment and create an atextual carveout for post-employment discrimination in employer-controlled benefits. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co., 519 U.S. 337 (1997), supports construing employment-discrimination protections to reach former employees where the statutory text does not clearly impose a temporal limitation, and nothing in § 12112(a) expressly restricts “privileges of employment” to decisions made during active service. Consistent with methodological coherence and Robinson’s contextual approach, Title I should be construed to allow a former employee to sue over discriminatory denial or reduction of post-employment benefits tied to the employment relationship.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Title I prohibits discrimination against a “qualified individual” in the “terms, conditions, and privileges of employment,” 42 U.S.C. § 12112(a), and employer-controlled retirement or pension benefits are quintessential “privileges of employment” earned through the employment relationship even if administered after separation. Reading “qualified individual” to categorically exclude former employees at the moment benefits are paid would create a practical loophole that permits disability discrimination precisely when benefits vest or are distributed, undermining the ADA’s remedial purpose and equal-protection values. Robinson v. Shell Oil Co. supports construing similar employment-discrimination language to reach post-employment actions affecting former employees, and nothing in § 12117(a)’s incorporation of Title VII enforcement suggests Congress intended a narrower, formalistic cutoff for ADA benefits claims. Procedural fairness and workable administration favor allowing suits where the challenged decision concerns benefits traceable to prior covered employment rather than requiring current job qualification unrelated to the benefit decision.
